sections.html:
Brantley County is a rural stretch of southeast Georgia with its seat at Nahunta. It covers roughly 442 square miles of mostly dry ground, with the Satilla River running through it. The population was 18,021 in 2020 and is about 18,936 by mid-2025. Homes have a middle value of $99,600, and 79.9 percent of housing is owner occupied for 2020 to 2024.

Just 77 building permits were issued in 2025, so new construction is thin. Most sellers are longtime owners of a single-family house, a tract of land or a mobile home. Density was 40.7 people per square mile in 2020, and 99.3 percent of residents lived in rural areas. Buyers tend to be local, and many properties are big lots or mobile home sites.

The Brantley County Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North in Nahunta, houses both property tax offices. One sends and collects the bills, and the other decides what each parcel is worth. Elected boards set the rate, so neither office can lower it.

The commissioner's site at brantleytax.com and the assessor's site at qpublic.net give details, and the county's tax offices page lists both numbers.

The commissioner's office now has a drive-through lane at the annex. You can request a mailing address change for a tax bill from the property record on its site.

The commissioner's office is responsible for ad valorem tax on these kinds of property:

  • Real property, meaning land and buildings
  • Personal property
  • Motor vehicles
  • Mobile homes
  • Timber

You can search any parcel and pay online through the same site. The news page carries tax sale notices, a list of excess funds and holiday closings. Look there before you list a home with unpaid years on it, since a parcel headed to tax sale is a hard sell.

The due date for the annual bill is printed on the bill itself. If yours is missing, phone 912-462-5723 and request both the due date and the amount needed to clear the account.

Keep a printout of the paid receipt for every year you own the property. Whoever handles the closing will want to see that earlier years are clear, and a receipt from the commissioner answers that at once.

Every schedule was updated in 2025 along with a full re-evaluation of all properties. The assessor keeps files on 13,406 real property parcels, 602 personal property accounts and 2,346 mobile homes without a homestead exemption.

Assessed value in Georgia is 40 percent of what a property was worth on January 1. Returns are taken from January 1 until April 1. An owner who files no return gets an assessment notice in mid-May, and that notice starts the appeal clock.

  • Submit a return before April 1 if you want to declare your own value
  • Open the notice as soon as it arrives and note the date it carries
  • Phone the assessor at 912-462-5251 with any questions while time remains

Because the re-evaluation changed values across the county, a home that looked cheap on paper a few years ago may now carry a noticeably different assessment. Pull the current record before you set a sale price.

Before listing, compare the county's record of your house with what is really there. Wrong square footage, a shed that was torn down or an addition that was never recorded are easier to fix before a buyer's appraiser spots them.

The assessment notice opens a 45-day window, and that is the only one you get. A challenge starts with the Board of Tax Assessors. Georgia's usual path then moves to the Board of Equalization and last to Superior Court, and arbitration is offered in place of the board hearing.

Grounds are value, uniformity and taxability. A complaint about the size of the bill does not count, since the bill follows the millage rate, which cannot be appealed.

  • Write the appeal out and keep your own copy
  • Collect recent nearby sales and any repair quotes
  • Ask the assessor how a hearing is requested

The count runs from the notice date, so a mailbox you rarely check can cost you days.

If you are about to sell, an appeal can still be worth filing when the assessed value looks too high, since a lower figure helps whoever owns the house on January 1. Tell your closing agent about any appeal still open, so the paperwork says who keeps a refund if one comes.

sections.h2: What local housing patterns mean for a seller
sections.html:
Listings are scarce and owners stay put. There are 6,599 households, and 94.3 percent of residents had not moved in the past year. Median gross rent is $755, and a mortgaged owner spends a median $1,087 monthly. Three practical points follow for anyone weighing a sale:

  • Family and inherited land is common, so check whose names appear on the deed and on the tax bill before you list.
  • Brantley is part of the Brunswick metropolitan area, and Wayne, Glynn, Camden, Charlton, Ware and Pierce counties touch it, so buyers often shop those neighbors too.
  • Nearly 19 percent of residents are 65 or older, so estate and heir questions come up often. After an owner's death, ask the probate court how to proceed.

Begin by getting a payoff amount from the tax commissioner, because unpaid county taxes must be cleared before a buyer can receive clean title. Then have the settlement agent work out each side's share of the year's bill.

If the house is a mobile home, confirm whether it is billed on its own or together with the land, since the assessor tracks non-homesteaded mobile homes as separate accounts. Homestead status affects this, so ask the assessor which treatment your home has.

Owners hurt by the Highway 82 fire can call the county commissioners' office at 912-462-5256, extension 5, about recovery resources. Ask the assessor how fire damage is reflected in your record before you price the property.

A short checklist for the office visit: bring your deed or parcel number, your latest bill and any receipts for earlier years. Ask for the payoff in writing with the date it is good through. A cash buyer who takes the property as it stands can close without repair demands or lender delays, though the tax balance is still paid out of your proceeds.

faqs.q: How can I pay my Brantley County tax bill?
faqs.a: Pay the tax commissioner, either online at brantleytax.com or in person at Suite D of the Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North, Nahunta. The office number is 912-462-5723, and it is open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30.

faqs.q: What is the appeal deadline for a Brantley County assessment?
faqs.a: The deadline is 45 days after the date printed on the notice, and it is firm. File in writing before it ends.

faqs.q: Does the Brantley County assessor set my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The assessor sets the value only. The county commissioners and the school board set millage rates, and the tax commissioner sends the bill.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Brantley County house if taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the back taxes are paid at or before closing so the buyer gets clear title. Request a payoff from the tax commissioner and make sure it appears on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: When are Brantley County property tax returns due?
faqs.a: Returns are taken from January 1 until April 1 each year. Owners who miss that cutoff receive assessment notices in mid-May, and the 45-day appeal period starts then.
